children.text: Fort San Andres is a 17th-century Spanish fort standing on San Antonio Hill behind Romblon town. From its square coral-stone walls you can look over Romblon Bay, the harbor and the town rooftops, and it is at its best around sunset.

Fort San Andres sits on a hill above Romblon town, the main town on Romblon Island. It stands on San Antonio Hill between Barangay II and Capaclan, and below it lies Romblon Bay, a natural harbor. The fort was originally one half of the Twin Forts of Romblon. It was built in the 17th century as a pair with Fort Santiago on Calvary Hill, but only Fort San Andres still keeps its wall outline intact, so it is the one visitors can actually climb.

Its history goes back to the early Spanish colonial period. Martín de Goiti first visited these islands in 1569, an encomienda was set up in 1571, and Romblon became a formal pueblo in 1631. Augustinian Recollect friars began their mission around 1635, and one of them, Fr. Agustin de San Pedro, led the construction of the fort starting in 1644. He even trained local people in self-defense, which earned him the nickname "El Padre Capitan." At the time Romblon suffered raids by Muslim pirates from Mindanao and attacks by the Dutch, and records mention that Dutch forces plundered and destroyed the town in 1646. The fort was built from coral and limestone that locals could gather easily, and some sources say it was completed and dedicated in 1650. Start and completion dates differ among sources, so it is best to think of it simply as a mid-17th-century fort.
The fort is a four-sided square with a turret at each corner. Its area is only about
290 m²

, so if you expect a huge citadel it may feel rather small. Each wall and turret has three embrasures where cannons once pointed out, and the main entrance is a wooden door in the south wall. On the side facing away from the sea, you can still see where four stone columns once held up a thatched roof. In 2012 the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) granted about

for work that included replacing coral stone, adding drainage, reinforcing the foundation, restoring the turrets and building protective riprap against erosion. In 2013 the National Museum declared the fort a National Cultural Treasure, together with other Romblon landmarks.

For travelers, this fort is less about "sights" than about views and atmosphere. A short climb, a lap around the walls, and time to take in Romblon Bay, the town rooftops and the boats in the harbor take only 1–2 hours. The fort grounds are also used by the Romblon observatory of PAGASA, the national weather agency, so modern equipment can be seen next to the old walls. It lies on the same hillside area as St. Joseph Cathedral in Romblon town, so the two make a good walking day together. The path up and the top of the walls can be rough, so early morning or late afternoon is better than the hot midday. Opening hours and entry arrangements also differ from one travel account to another, so plan on checking on arrival. The fort itself is small, but it explains the history and layout of the town that serves as the starting point for the Romblon islands, so it is worth half a day at the start or end of your island trip.

blocks.title: Coral-stone walls and four corner turrets

children.text: Walls piled from blocks of coral and limestone run in a square, with a turret at every corner. Each parapet has three gun openings, so you can see for yourself how cannons once aimed at the harbor.
From the walls you can take in Romblon Bay, the natural harbor, the town rooftops and passing boats at a glance. The view makes it easy to see why the Spanish chose this hill.
You can watch the sun go down over the western sea from the walls. However, one travel account says the caretaker may close the gate before sunset, so it is safest to go up about
1 hour
before the sun sets.
Reviews say the staircase is lined with gardens, hedges and statues. True to Romblon's reputation as a marble island, stone carvings stand out. The steps are steep, so wear comfortable shoes.

This fort originally formed a pair with Fort Santiago on Calvary Hill. Fort Santiago is now a ruin covered by soil, grass and bushes and is hard to make out, so be content to imagine the whole twin-fort story from Fort San Andres.

The walls were repaired through the 2012 restoration project and the 2013 National Cultural Treasure declaration. A local citizens' group has worked to protect the fort, and the donation collected at entry is known to go toward its upkeep.

The fort grounds also hold the Romblon observatory of PAGASA, the Philippine weather agency. It is not a tourist facility, so follow staff instructions before taking photos near the equipment or going in.

Climb the steep stairs for about
5–10 minutes
, then pay the donation at the fort entrance and go in.
Walk around the top of the walls and photograph Romblon Bay, the harbor and the town rooftops.
Come down before dark and watch the sunset from a spot with a view of the western sky. Watch the closing time.
Return to town, see the exterior of St. Joseph Cathedral and have dinner at a restaurant near the harbor.

The most common way to reach Romblon Island from Manila is to travel by plane or bus to a port such as Batangas and take a boat. Romblon Port is the gateway to the town.

If flights are available, you can also land on Tablas Island and cross to Romblon Island by boat. Routes, schedules and fares change often, so check airline and shipping-line announcements just before you leave.
We could not confirm exact ferry schedules. Boats are often canceled in bad weather, so leave at least one extra day in your schedule.

items.title: From Romblon Port to the fort stairs

children.text: The fort is inside Romblon town, so you can walk from near the port or take a motorcycle or tricycle to the foot of the stairs. The stair entrance is on the Termopilas Street side, and a narrow road from Sabang Road is also said to lead up to it.
The climb is steep and takes
5–10 minutes
. Bring water on hot days.
The town is small, so you can walk to most sights, with tricycles and motorcycle taxis as backup. Check fares locally.
Romblon is classified as having no pronounced wet or dry season, but rain is generally heavier from June to December and drier from January to May. The average annual temperature is about
and annual rainfall is reported as roughly 2,400-2,800 mm depending on the source (about 2,378 mm in PAGASA 1991-2020 normals, about 2,845 mm on a weather site).

Climbing the fort is far easier in the dry season than in the rainy season, when wet steps get slippery. For sunset, March to May has clear skies, but the midday sun is strong, so go up in the late afternoon.

Romblon town has small lodgings and restaurants clustered around the harbor. Staying in town lets you revisit the fort and cathedral at dawn and dusk. Lodging names and rates change by season, so compare booking sites and recent local reviews before choosing.

Food is mostly Filipino home cooking built around seafood and rice. Marble is Romblon's signature product, so souvenir shops sell many marble items. Think about transport and airline baggage weight before buying heavy marble.

Romblon is a long trip from Manila, so rather than staying one night, it is better to stay two or more nights and combine the town, nearby beaches and island tours. The town goes quiet early at night and may have few money-exchange or ATM options, so bring the cash you need in advance and ask your lodging about electricity and mobile signal. The fort works well as a light stop between other town activities.
